articles.title: Public health reform
articles.content: TWO weeks ago, I participated in the Georgetown Pakistan Forum in Washington, DC, organised by Pakistani students at the university. The forum brings together policymakers, business leaders, technologists, academics, students and diaspora representatives to discuss Pakistan’s future and promote evidence-based policies, public-private partnerships and solutions for Pakistan and its 1.2 million-strong Pakistani-American diaspora. I acknowledge the two student leaders who, with their passionate team, organised the event: Rai Hasen Masoud of the School of Foreign Service, president of the Georgetown South Asian Society, and Shahaan Shafi of the School of Health, president of its Academic Council. Seven policy working groups covered com-munity health, maternal health, defence and strategic stability, democracy and gover-nance, critical minerals and energy, technology for finance and education, and health financing and infrastructure. Pakistan’s public health crisis is the consequence of political choices and misplaced priorities. Public health was a recurring theme during the forum. I participated in two working groups, a panel discussion and the concluding plenary, where I spoke about reforming public health in Pakistan. Here is my argument. The WHO defines public health as the art and science of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting health through the organised efforts of society. Pakistan’s public health situation is a crisis. Consider a few indicators. Our population is growing at 2.4 per cent annually, while the total fertility rate is 3.6. We add a population more than that of New Zealand every year. Meanwhile, economic growth in 2025-26 is projected at 3.65pc, barely exceeding population growth. This leaves little room for per capita prosperity to improve. Maternal and child health indicators are troubling. Pakistan has the world’s second-highest neonatal mortality rate, while approximately half of women of reproductive age suffer from anaemia. A quarter of our children remain unvaccinated against vaccine-preventable diseases. Pakistan remains one of only two countries where polio cases persist, obstructing global eradication efforts. We also have the world’s largest hepatitis C burden, Asia’s fastest-growing HIV epidemic, increasingly spreading beyond high-risk groups, and the fifth-largest tuberculosis burden globally. The situation is no better regarding non-communicable diseases. Every third adult above 18 suffers from type-2 diabetes, while every fourth adult above 40 has hypertension. Both increase risks of cardiovascular disease, stroke and kidney complications. Lifestyle medicine needs to be integrated at all levels of the healthcare system. Mental health remains the most neglected area, with limited access to appropriate care. What went wrong, particularly when so many of these conditions are preventable? The answer lies in decades of government neglect, chronic underinvestment, an overwhelming emphasis on curative healthcare, growing social inequity and poverty, and failure to develop a strong primary healthcare system. Can we reverse this situation? Certainly. Other countries have demonstrated that progress is possible. This requires political commitment and 10 reforms. First, government spending on health should progressively move towards the WHO-recommended benchmark of 5pc of GDP. Health must become a fiscal priority. Essential public health programmes, including immunisation, HIV and TB control, should be sustainably financed through domestic resources rather than continued dependence on development partners. Emergency preparedness also requires adequate investment. Second, generalist bureaucracy has increasingly become a constraint on health sector development. Pakistan’s Central Superior Services comprises 12 occupational groups, but health is not among them. Ministries of health should be led predominantly by technically qualified professionals, supported by competent administrators. Third, the 18th Constitutional Amendment devolved health responsibilities to provinces, but national coordination has weakened. Health challenges do not respect administrative boundaries. Common standards, surveillance, disease-control strategies, global health commitments and emergency preparedness require effective intergovernmental coordination. Fourth, Pakistan needs a National Health Service (NHS) framework to ensure integrated healthcare delivery, bringing public and private providers together. Drawing lessons from the UK’s NHS, we should institutionalise public-private partnerships to expand access, improve quality and make better use of existing resources. Fifth, primary healthcare must be strengthened. Prevention, early diagnosis and health promotion should form the foundation of our healthcare system. These services belong primarily at community and primary-care levels, not in tertiary hospitals. This requires empowered district health departments, functional facilities and a stronger focus on preventive and promotive services. Sixth, we need to rationalise our health workforce through better planning of its size, distribution and skills. Medical education must respond to national healthcare needs, with appropriate proportions of doctors, nurses, allied health professionals and community health workers. Seventh, responsible use of digital technologies and AI can improve health information systems, strengthen governance, expand access through telemedicine and standardise care. These investments must be guided by equity, accountability and data protection. Eighth, patient safety and quality must become priorities, supported by stronger regulatory standards and enforcement. Healthcare should heal, not harm. Effective infection prevention and control, safe injections and blood transfusions are essential. The transmission of hepatitis C and HIV through unsafe medical practices demonstrates the consequences of neglecting patient safety. Ninth, we must engage the Pakistani medical diaspora through a coherent government policy that institutionalises mechanisms to mobilise the expertise, experience, technology and investment of health professionals abroad. Tenth, we must strengthen intersectoral action. Health is shaped well beyond hospitals and health facilities. Environmental pollution, climate change, food systems, urban planning, education and lifestyle behaviours all influence health outcomes. The health sector must lead collaboration to address these wider determinants. Pakistan’s public health crisis is not inevitable. It is the consequence of political choices, misplaced priorities and institutional weaknesses. What is required is a shift from treating illness to protecting and promoting health. The challenge is not simply to spend more on healthcare, but to govern better, invest wisely and build a system that puts people and prevention first. The writer is a former health minister, adjunct professor of health systems and president of Pakistan Association of Lifestyle Medicine.
articles.author: Zafar Mirza

articles.title: More credit, fewer women
articles.content: IMAGINE Sakina, up at the crack of dawn to go see her precious Billo, a fine cow her father had given her. This would be Sakina’s 30th day selling Billo’s milk to a nearby farm owner who wanted good milk for his young children. She was excited to get paid. She got ready to head out, feeling like a businesswoman. Three years later, Sakina has four animals. She feeds them, looks after them and gets the milk ready for collection. She knows when a cow is giving less milk, when feed becomes heavier on the pocket and when it makes sense to buy another animal. Her 40-plus customers know how rich the milk is. But ask them where it comes from and they’ll tell you it’s from Kareem bhai, the doodh wala. Kareem is Sakina’s husband. He delivers the milk and his name is also the one on the ledger that she has maintained all these years. Sakina is sure she could manage 10 animals. She decides to start with two more cows and goes to a bank for a loan. That’s when the name in the ledger becomes a problem. She has years of milk sales to show the bank. She’s kept the records herself but they are in Kareem’s name. The bank decides against giving her a loan. Pakistan’s agricultural lending ambitions must look beyond the size of the portfolio. The State Bank of Pakistan’s Banking on Equalityfigures showthat agricultural financing to women rose from Rs44 billion in 2021 to Rs105bn in 2025 in nominal terms. In those same years, the number of women agricultural borrowers fell from 436,000 to 377,000, a decline of about 14 per cent. The data doesn’t show why fewer women borrowed or who received the additional financing. Yet the amounts lent more than doubled while the number of women borrowers fell. That matters for Banking on Equality 2026. The policy asks banks and development finance institutions to aim to double their financing portfolios for women and qualifying women-owned or women-led businesses across priority sectors by the end of 2028. A bank can grow its loan book by lending more to people it already knows. Reaching a woman like Sakina takes a closer look at who’s been running the business all these years. Agriculture accounts for roughly 23pc of Pakistan’s GDP, and livestock makes up nearly two-thirds of the sector’s value added. The Labour Force Survey 2024-25 tells us that about six in 10 employed women work in agriculture, forestry or fishing. What’s harder to see is who gets paid for that work and who decides how the money is spent. Take three women who look after cattle. One is paid a wage. Another tends the family’s animals and earns no income of her own. The third runs a dairy business like Sakina’s. To decide if a loan makes sense, a bank needs to understand how each woman earns her living and how much of that income she can use to repay it. Sakina’s milk delivery records could give the bank a place to start. Then come the questions she already asks herself. How much does feed cost? What happens to her income when a cow stops producing milk? What does she already owe? Banking on Equality encourages banks to consider evidence like this when assessing women-owned and women-led businesses. There’s one question the loan officer needs to ask a woman like Sakina directly. When the buyer pays for the milk, who can use that money? A buyer could put the supplier account in her name tomorrow and still hand the cash to Kareem. If the loan is in her name, the bank will expect her to pay it back. Can she decide where to sell the milk and set aside enough for the next instalment? In Kenya, CGAP documented how Agrilife and New Kenya Cooperative Creameries used digital delivery records to help dairy suppliers get advances against milk they’d already delivered. A separate study of two Kenyan dairy cooperatives found that farmers short of cash or facing uninsured health expenses shifted sales towards buyers who paid on the spot. Financing a cow means working out what it might produce in the future. And records kept in a farmer group’s name may tell a bank very little about what one woman sold. Could we use the records buyers already keep to show what women like Sakina actually sell and earn? A provincial livestock department could bring milk buyers and banks together to work with women who already run dairy businesses and want to expand. Ask buyers to record what each woman delivers and what she’s paid. If she wants to be paid into an account, let her choose one she can operate herself. If the money is paid in cash or through several buyers, the department maintains a record. With her consent, the bank can use those records alongside its usual checks and see whether they change its decision. After a year, we should know whether banks approved applications they would previously have declined and whether more women received payments directly. We can follow the loan cycles for longer too. Could the women keep up with repayments? After feed, veterinary bills and instalments, did they have more income left? Could they decide what to do with it? SBP can do something now. Put the amount lent and the number of individual women who borrowed on the same page. Show how many took out a formal loan for the first time and where borrower numbers are falling. Sakina knows the business and what it will take to grow it. She went to the bank to get support but came back without a loan or a clear way forward. When the banks report back in 2028, we should look at how many women like Sakina got far enough to have someone sit down with them and assess their potential for growth. Sakina may still look at the instalment and decide to wait. But that should be her decision to make. The writer leads the women’s economic and digital inclusion portfolio at Karandaaz Pakistan. The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of Karandaaz Pakistan.
articles.author: Samia Salik

articles.title: Constitutional liability
articles.content: EVERY out-of-school child is a living reminder to the state of its constitutional commitment, and these reminders have been increasing since the inception of Pakistan. Now these living reminders have crossed 25 million. Seventy-nine years after independence, Pakistan is still struggling to fulfil one of the most fundamental responsibilities of a modern state, ensuring that every child receives an education. A nuclear state has produced generations without an education system capable of accommodating them. Pakistan’s failure to educate its children is not a recent phenomenon, nor did the constitutional responsibility of the state begin with Article 25-A in 2010. The commitment dates back to the country’s early constitutional history. The 1956 Constitution explicitly recognised the state’s responsibility to eliminate illiteracy and provide free and compulsory primary education. The 1962 Constitution retained this commitment. The 1973 Constitution went further through Article 37(b), requiring the state to remove illiteracy and provide free and compulsory secondary education within the minimum possible period. The insertion of Article 25-A through the 18th Constitutional Amendment in 2010 was therefore not the beginning of the state’s educational responsibility. It was an attempt to transform a longstanding constitutional aspiration into an enforceable fundamental right. Yet, decades of constitutional commitments have failed to produce universal educational access. From the promise of compulsory primary education in 1956 to the guarantee of education for every child aged 5-16 in 2010, the state has repeatedly renewed its commitment without ensuring its fulfilment. Every child denied education represents lost human capital. The question is why, despite repeated constitutional commitments, successive governments have failed to ensure that every child has access to a school. It seems every government has also failed to realise that every child denied education represents lost human capital and another potential victim of intergenerational poverty. A country cannot build a knowledge economy, strengthen democratic institutions, or achieve sustainable development while leaving millions of its children disconnected from education and the opportunities that accompany it. The children are not the liability. The liability is created by a system that allows millions of children to grow up without education, skills, opportunities, or meaningful participation in society. Unesco data indicates that Pakistan has a substantially higher proportion of primary-school-age children out of school compared with India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, the Maldives, and Sri Lanka. While these countries have made considerable progress in expanding educational access, Pakistan continues to struggle with millions of children excluded from the education system. This regional disparity suggests that the crisis is not merely a consequence of poverty or population growth, but also reflects persistent failures of educational planning, governance, investment and political commitment. Bringing over 25m out-of-school children into the education system is not merely a matter of an enrolment campaign. It requires an enormous expansion of educational infrastructure, human resources and recurring public expenditure. Assuming 40 students per classroom, Pakistan would need approximately 628,750 classrooms to accommodate these children. At an illustrative staffing ratio of 1.2 teachers per classroom, the country would require approximately 754,500 additional teachers. If these teachers were recruited at the initial BPS-14 pay of Rs27,060 per month, the annual salary bill alone would be roughly Rs245 billion. This estimate covers basic salaries only, excludes allowances, pensions, and teacher training. The capital cost of constructing schools with basic amenities, as well as recurring administrative expenditure, would certainly be a substantially higher fiscal commitment. The scale of the challenge is enormous, so is the cost of inaction. Pakistan’s reported education expenditure of Rs962bn in FY2024-25 was already insufficient to meet the needs of its existing education system. The question is therefore not simply how much it would cost to educate the excluded children, but why a country that has constitutionally guaranteed education to every child has failed to develop a sustainable financing mechanism to fulfil that guarantee. A constitutional right cannot remain confined to the pages of a constitution, nor can the state continue to measure its educational achievements through policies announced, schools inaugurated, or budgets allocated. The real measure of its commitment must be the child sitting in a classroom, learning to read, write, think, and participate in society. The writer is a social development practitioner.
articles.author: Aamir Latif Siddiqui

articles.title: Beyond our means
articles.content: IT is unfortunate that most people in Pakistan spend more than they earn. It is a fact that inflation is seriously diminishing the public’s buying power and adversely impacting whatever savings they have. In this scenario, people should think about changing their lifestyle and focusing on saving more. This argument is supported by the fact that Pakistan has one of the highest rates of consumer borrowing for non-productive purposes in South Asia. People are not borrowing to start a business; they are borrowing to maintain certain lifestyles. Pakistan’s domestic savings ratio is one of the lowest in the world. It dropped from 17.4 per cent of GDP in 1992 to just 6.4pc in 2024, the weakest in a generation and far lower than countries in the region. Pakistan’s 30-year average savings is 10.9pc of GDP. Bangladesh’s average is approximately 21pc, India’s is around 28pc, and Vietnam’s is around 30pc. People should realise that whatever they earn is their own property, but rash spending habits are damaging for themselves and also for the country. The nation’s overall poor savings habits are also a critical reason for the state’s reliance on loans from global donors. Pakistan’s savings ratio has fallen massively in the last 30 years because domestic lifestyles have changed. Parents of past generations knew how to say no. Yet many parents of today proudly fulfil their child’s every wish, come what may. This type of thinking has played a part in making people live beyond their means. If parents really love their children, they should focus on fulfilling their actual needs, which are food, clothes, education and health. All things other than these basics are actually demands. Pakistan’s domestic savings ratio is one of the lowest in the world. Good parenting involves fulfilling children’s needs and managing their demands in a rational manner. A good parent believes that he or she earns for their children, and it is his or her responsibility to secure their future by making sacrifices in the present. We as a nation make wrong spending choices in our daily routines while during weddings and funerals, spending tends to go haywire because of social pressures. For weddings, many families spend beyond their means to keep up with the Joneses. Pakistan’s average monthly income is Rs40,000-80,000, but an average marriage easily costs Rs1.5 million to Rs2.5m, which is equivalent to three to five years’ total salary for a middle-class parent or guardian. Dowry is another burden for a bride’s family. It is unfortunate that 13.5m women in Pakistan are unmarried because their families cannot afford dowry-related expenses. It is unfortunate that even after giving dowry, the greed of some remains unfulfilled, and they do not shy away from harming the bride whose dowry is not as per their expectations. According to the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, more than 2,000 women die each year in dowry-related disputes. More than 1.6m marriages take place in Pakistan annually, and more than Rs110 billion is spent on these weddings every year. Marriages are happy occasions, but even during moments of grief, such as a death in the family, unnecessary expenditures are made, because of various rituals. As these examples illustrate, living beyond one’s means appears to be the daily economic behaviour of the nation. Moreover, a middle-class family pays 30pc-40pc of its income to private schools and private hospitals because the government is unable to provide the basic rights of health and education to the people. The majority of the population is relying on private setups for health and education, and this segment is eating up a large chunk of income. The world is becoming unstable, and wars are now becoming the new norm. These conflicts are not only impacting the countries involved but are also having an adverse effect on the availability and pricing of global resources, such as oil and gas. In this changing scenario, it is highly critical that awareness campaigns be launched at all levels to highlight the benefits of savings. The public should be convinced to bring simplicity into their lives. Chapters about the benefits of savings and living with simplicity should be included in the curriculum and be propagated through social media platforms. It is also incumbent on the state to improve health and education facilities, particularly for the lower-income bracket. Saving is a good habit. Even religion has preached moderation. Those who prepare for the worst in good times reap the benefit in the long run. It is high time that the nation should learn from its past errors and reset its spending habits to bring stability in the present and to secure its future.
articles.author: Khurram Zia Khan

articles.title: Opposition disarray
articles.content: THE PTI on Wednesdaydistanceditself from Mahmood Khan Achakzai’s proposal for a national government and his demand for political and constitutional reforms. The party has not issued a formal reaction, but its leaders have made its stance clear in background conversations with the media. This shows the alliance chief did not consult other parties beforemaking the proposal public. A similar disconnect between the PTI and other member parties of the TTAP surfaced a couple of months ago, when the PTI gave a call for a protest march on Islamabad. Speaking at a conference in Lahore, Mr Achakzai also stressed constitutional supremacy, parliamentary sovereignty and the restoration of democracy. His concerns about worsening insecurity in KP, Balochistan and AJK deserve serious attention. These problems will not be solved by unilateral decisions or political expediency. However, the demand for a national government appears premature and offers no clear way out of political uncertainty. Replacing the present setup with an arrangement whose mandate and duration remain undefined could deepen existing divisions. More concerning is the opposition alliance’s lack of coordination, which has again exposed its differences. Opposition parties need to settle whether their leaders speak for the alliance or only for their own parties. Contradicting one another in public weakens their credibility. A coalition that cannot agree on a public position will struggle to offer a credible alternative programme. The opposition would be better off using the rest of the parliamentary term to press the government on issues that bear directly on democratic governance. These issues include protection of civil liberties, curbs on freedom of expression and the matter of political prisoners. The restoration of normal democratic administration in KP also requires attention. Moreover, both sides of the aisle need to begin working out arrangements to ensure free, fair and credible elections when the present government’s term ends. That requires agreement on electoral safeguards, the neutrality of state institutions and an environment in which parties can compete without intimidation. Calls for constitutional supremacy will carry little weight unless political parties show their own commitment to parliamentary democracy. Sustained engagement in parliament would help the opposition build public confidence, and it should not squander that chance on premature demands for another political arrangement. The government would do well to reckon with the cost of poor governance, heavy-handed treatment of the opposition and other sections of society, and a weak economic record. Left unaddressed, these issues will hand its critics ample ammunition for more agitation.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Revamping audits
articles.content: THE government’s decision to overhaul the audit system is long overdue. Weak audit oversight has undermined confidence in corporate financial reporting, discouraged investment and weakened accountability across the economy. The concerns raised by the Prime Minister’s FBR Task Force deserve serious attention. Investors, lenders and regulators depend on audited financial statements to assess the financial health of companies. When those statements cannot be trusted, the entire investment environment suffers. The country’s failure to meet international standards for independent audit oversight is particularly damaging. The International Organisation of Securities Commissions has declared Pakistan non-compliant with these requirements. The EU has also withdrawn its equivalence status for independent audit oversight. These setbacks should have prompted corrective action much earlier. The proposed amendments to the SECP law and the Audit Oversight Board framework are therefore welcome. Greater independence for the oversight board, restrictions on members having links with audit firms and regular risk-based inspections could improve accountability. Giving the board powers to investigate complaints and pursue suspected falsification should also strengthen enforcement. However, changing laws and creating regulatory powers will not automatically produce credible audits. The question is whether the new arrangements can withstand pressure from influential companies, audit firms and other vested interests. Replacing one professional group’s dominance with greater state influence would hardly constitute reform. There is also a wider problem that cannot be ignored. Pakistan’s public-sector audit system suffers from similar weaknesses. An IMF governance assessment last year highlighted the Auditor General’s limited independence, staff shortages and poor parliamentary follow-up. Thousands of pages of audit reports have produced little corrective action. This illustrates a fundamental weakness in the country’s approach to accountability. Audit findings frequently expose irregularities, but those responsible rarely face timely consequences. The government must ensure that corporate audit reform does not become just another exercise in legislative compliance.
articles.author: Editorial
